# Why LPs Keep Catching Your Track-Record Restatements


Your IRR figures can be completely accurate and still land as a discrepancy if two documents going to the same LP reflect different data pulls from different weeks. That's the gap LP diligence teams are trained to find, and automated scoring models are now catching it before a human reviewer even opens the file. The fix lives upstream of the submission itself, in how your performance data gets stored and approved before it reaches anyone.


**TLDR:**


- LP financial due diligence on private funds tests whether your track record is internally consistent across every channel, beyond whether returns are strong
- Subscription line adjustments alone can shift a reported IRR from 26% to 37% on the same deal, making methodology disclosure a requirement, not a courtesy
- LP consultants rebuild IRR from raw cash flows and cross-reference every DDQ against prior submissions going back multiple fund cycles
- Two or more red flags in one submission cycle, such as unexplained IRR variance between your DDQ and pitch book, typically trigger a data room reconciliation request before any recommendation advances
- GovernGPT stores each performance figure with an approval date and an as-of date, propagating updates across all outbound DDQ and RFP answers so conflicting versions cannot surface across submissions


## What Financial Due Diligence Means for a Private Fund


Financial due diligence on a private fund is not the same exercise as transaction diligence on a company. When an institutional allocator assesses a GP before committing capital, the question is not whether the underlying assets are fairly priced. The question is whether the manager can be trusted with the money at all.


For LPs, financial due diligence means systematically reviewing a GP's track record, performance reporting methodology, and the internal controls that govern how financial data gets produced and disclosed. It covers how returns are calculated, whether fee and expense treatment is consistent across vintages, how valuations are supported, and whether the numbers presented today match what was reported in prior cycles. The primary instruments for this process are DDQs and RFPs, supported by a range of[LP due diligence tools](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/top-lp-due-diligence-tools-gps-scaling) , where GPs are expected to answer detailed questions about performance, fund structure, and financial governance under their own signature.


What sets this apart from other forms of diligence is the reliance on self-reported data. A GP controls what goes into their track record presentation. The LP's job is to test whether that presentation is internally consistent, methodologically sound, and reconcilable with independently verifiable sources. That is the core problem financial due diligence is designed to solve.


## The Five Dimensions LPs Assess During Fund Manager Due Diligence


Institutional LPs run a structured review process, and track-record data is only one layer of it. Understanding where performance figures sit within the broader framework helps IR teams anticipate what gets questioned and why.


There are five dimensions that consistently appear across LP due diligence frameworks, each carrying distinct weight in the allocation decision.


### Investment Track Record


Gross and net returns by vintage, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, and the methodology behind each, the same figures covered in a thorough[DDQ performance section](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/ddq-performance-section-irr-moic-tvpi-guide) . LPs want to reconstruct the numbers independently, never simply accept them as presented.


### Organizational Stability


Key-person concentration, team tenure, ownership structure, and recent departures. A strong track record attached to a team that has since fractured carries less weight than allocators might have accepted in prior cycles.


### Back-Office Infrastructure


Back-office systems, fund administration setup, valuation governance, and the controls that sit between raw portfolio data and what gets reported to LPs.[Fund infrastructure due diligence](https://carta.com/learn/private-funds/management/fund-administration/operational-due-diligence/) has grown in weight; sophisticated allocators now treat it as a near-equal counterpart to investment diligence.


### Compliance Posture


Regulatory history, marketing materials review, and whether disclosed policies match observed practice. Inconsistencies between what a GP says in a DDQ and what appears in their ADV or prior filings get flagged quickly.


### Financial Reporting Integrity


Whether figures are consistent across submissions, whether expense treatment is disclosed and applied uniformly, and whether the GP can explain discrepancies between gross and net performance across vintages. This is where track-record restatements tend to surface, and it is the dimension that carries the most reputational weight when something does not add up.


## How Performance Data Gets Reported Across a Fundraising Cycle


Performance data does not live in one place. A GP raising a new fund simultaneously manages a pitch deck, a DDQ, a quarterly investor letter, a one-pager for placement agents, and recurring questionnaires from existing LPs monitoring prior commitments. The same core figures, gross IRR, net IRR, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, realized and unrealized values, must appear consistently across all of them.


Each channel has its own update cadence. A quarterly letter reflects portfolio values as of a specific quarter-end. A DDQ submitted two months later may draw from a different data pull. A pitch deck, often built once and revised sporadically, can carry figures that predate both. When an LP's diligence team cross-references these documents, as they routinely do, any gap between channels becomes a question that requires an explanation.


Across a multi-year fundraising cycle, the exposure compounds. A GP raising Fund V will face LPs who have Fund III and Fund IV DDQ responses on file. If the reported net IRR for Fund III shifted between the Fund IV raise and the Fund V raise without an accompanying explanation about subscription line methodology or realization timing, that shift registers as a discrepancy, not a refinement.


## Why Track-Record Numbers Shift Between Submissions


Several mechanisms explain why performance figures shift between submissions, and most of them are structural, not intentional.


### Subscription Credit Facility Adjustments


This is the most common source of IRR variance across fund cycles. The IRR effect is material: subscription line adjustments alone can shift a reported IRR from 26% to 37% on the same deal, depending on draw timing and facility size. As[ILPA's 2017 subscription line guidance](https://ilpa.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/ILPA-Subscription-Lines-of-Credit-and-Alignment-of-Interests-June-2017.pdf) noted, these facilities had expanded well beyond short-term bridging functions into broader cash management tools. When a GP discloses subscription-line-adjusted figures in one submission and gross-of-line figures in another, the headline IRR moves, and LPs notice.


### Realized vs. Unrealized Reclassifications


As portfolio companies exit, unrealized value converts to realized distributions. A net IRR figure from 18 months ago may have included a company now fully realized at a different multiple. When the reclassification changes the blended return without an explicit note, the prior figure looks inconsistent.


### Data Source Fragmentation


The most unglamorous cause is also the most common: a DDQ team pulls figures from a different spreadsheet version than the one used for the prior submission, a gap that proper[waterfall and DDQ reconciliation](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/waterfall-lpa-fund-returns-ddq-reconciliation) is meant to prevent. Waterfall models get updated. Fund admin exports get refreshed. A co-investment figure gets reclassified. Without a single governed data source, these routine updates produce numbers that do not align with what was previously filed.


## The ILPA DDQ and What It Actually Demands From GPs on Performance


The[ILPA DDQ 2.0](https://ilpa.org/industry-guidance/templates-standards-model-documents/due-diligence-questionnaire-and-diversity-metrics-template/) , last updated in November 2021 and still the current published version as of this writing, is the de facto institutional standard for LP due diligence on fund managers. Most sophisticated allocators either use it directly or build their own questionnaires around its structure.


The DDQ requires fund-level performance templates covering gross and net returns by vintage, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, and the methodology behind each figure. Portfolio investment templates go further, asking GPs to break down returns at the deal level: entry and exit dates, cost basis, realized and unrealized value, and the gross IRR attributable to each investment. GP-led secondaries and continuation funds get their own appendix, reflecting how LP scrutiny has followed the evolution of GP liquidity strategies.


What makes this demanding from a data-integrity standpoint is the cross-referencing it invites. A GP completing both the fund template and the portfolio investment template in the same submission is filing two sets of numbers that must match. If the fund-level net IRR implies a distribution profile inconsistent with the deal-level realized values, a diligent LP will find it.


## The SEC Marketing Rule and Recordkeeping Obligations for Performance Data


Under the[SEC's Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1)](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/division-investment-management-frequently-asked-questions/marketing-compliance-frequently-asked-questions) , registered investment advisers must maintain records substantiating any performance figures presented to prospective investors. That requirement covers materials distributed through every channel: DDQs, pitch decks, one-pagers, and quarterly letters.


When figures shift between submissions, a restated IRR raises a recordkeeping question. Which version of that figure is supported by contemporaneous documentation, and what explains the variance? If the answer requires reconstructing a data trail after the fact, the firm has a compliance exposure that a fund admin export alone cannot resolve.


Every figure that reaches a prospective investor under a registered adviser's signature needs a defensible, documented source at the time it is distributed. That requires a governed recordkeeping architecture tying each disclosed figure to a specific approved source, with a timestamp.


## How LPs and Investment Consultants Catch Discrepancies


LP diligence teams do not read a DDQ submission in isolation. They read it against everything else the GP has produced.


The standard cross-referencing workflow pulls together the current DDQ, prior-year DDQ answers, the pitch deck, quarterly letters sent during the fund's life, and ADV filings. Investment consultants running diligence for pension funds and endowments typically add a proprietary comparison layer: their own database of prior submissions from the same GP, sometimes going back several fund cycles. When a figure in the current DDQ does not match what that GP reported two years ago, the consultant flags it and requests a written explanation before the recommendation advances.


The most technically rigorous step is rebuilding IRR from raw cash flows. In one illustrative case documented in[Compound Research's buyout fund DDQ walkthrough](https://getcompound.ai/use-cases/fund-due-diligence) , rebuilding from cash flows shifted a reported net IRR from 14.5% to 11.8% once subscription line effects were stripped out. A GP who has not anticipated that question in their DDQ answers is already behind.


Narrative inconsistencies get flagged alongside numerical ones, a common[RFP consistency failure](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/ai-rfp-consistency-failure-lps) in LP-facing materials. A DDQ describing a disciplined, concentrated strategy while the pitch deck references a broad sector mandate raises a question no IRR reconciliation resolves. One contradicted claim is enough to slow an otherwise qualified commitment to a second round of questions.


## Red Flags That Trigger Deeper LP Scrutiny of Performance Data


Not every discrepancy triggers a follow-up question. LPs have learned to distinguish between routine data refreshes and patterns that suggest something structural is off. The patterns below tend to escalate.


Red Flag Root Cause Typical LP Response


IRR differs between DDQ and pitch book with no explanatory footnote Figures drawn from different data pulls or document versions Immediate follow-up required before process advances


Realized returns shift between submission cycles without methodology note Exit reclassification not disclosed; silence treated as a gap Written explanation requested before recommendation advances


Gross-to-net spread inconsistent across strategies in the same fund family Fee and expense allocation applied unevenly across vintages Explicit disclosure of fee treatment demanded


MOIC calculations handle recycled capital differently across fund vintages No standardized recycling treatment applied across cycles Cross-vintage MOIC reconciliation requested


Subscription line footnote in pitch deck absent from DDQ Selective disclosure across channels; not a formatting error Flagged as selective disclosure; data room reconciliation likely


LP Red Flags: Performance Data Patterns That Trigger Deeper Scrutiny


- IRR figures that differ between the DDQ and the pitch book, with no footnote explaining the variance, is a textbook example of[DDQ answer inconsistency](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/lp-answer-inconsistency-ddq) . Two documents, one GP, two numbers: that requires an answer before the process moves forward.
- Realized returns that shift between submission cycles without an accompanying explanation. A figure can legitimately change as exits close, but when no methodology note accompanies the change, reviewers treat the silence as a gap and not an update.
- Gross-to-net spreads that are inconsistent across strategies within the same fund family. If the gap between gross and net IRR is 400 basis points in one strategy and 900 in another, the allocation of fees and expenses needs to be explained explicitly.
- MOIC calculations that handle recycled capital differently across fund vintages. Recycling treatment is a named source of MOIC variance, and LPs with multiple fund cycles on file will catch it.
- Attribution footnotes that appear in one document but are absent in another. A footnote disclosing subscription line usage in the pitch deck that does not appear in the DDQ reads as selective disclosure, not a formatting inconsistency.


Two or more of these in the same submission cycle frequently trigger a request for a data room reconciliation before the recommendation advances.


## Why Inconsistencies Happen: The Root Cause Is Data Infrastructure, Not Intent


Two analysts, two deadlines, two data pulls from two different spreadsheet versions. Neither pulled the wrong number. Both worked from the best available source at the time.


That is the structural problem. Thorough[fund manager due diligence preparation](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/fund-manager-due-diligence-ir-preparation) starts with recognizing that performance figures at most fund managers do not live in a single governed location. Waterfall models sit with the finance team. Fund admin exports arrive from a third party on a quarterly cadence. Historical DDQ responses are in a shared drive, sometimes versioned, sometimes not.


When a DDQ deadline arrives, an IR analyst pulls from whatever is accessible. Three weeks later, a different person updates the pitch deck from a different export. No one fabricated anything. But the figures do not match, and an LP's consultant database will surface that gap before anyone on the GP side notices it exists.


This is a data governance failure, not a values failure. Tighter review and more senior sign-off treat the symptom. The root cause is the absence of a single, version-controlled, timestamped source that all outbound materials draw from. Without that infrastructure, discrepancies are not an occasional risk. They are the expected output of a process built on fragmented inputs.


Manually tagged content libraries make this worse. Tags structure data for human retrieval, so every refreshed figure depends on someone re-tagging the right entries, and when the analyst who built the taxonomy leaves, the library starts to decay with them. That keyman risk is how a superseded net IRR ends up sitting in an "approved" library looking current. GovernGPT removes the dependency: it ingests Word, Excel, and PDF files in their original format, extracts approval date, fund, strategy, and LP at upload, and tags and maintains the data autonomously. The controlled vocabulary is generated by the system, so it does not leave when a person does.


## Building a Single Source of Truth for Performance Data Across LP Submissions


A single source of truth for performance data means one governed location where each figure, net IRR, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, gross-to-net spread, subscription-line-adjusted return, lives under version control with a dated approval attached to it. Every outbound document, DDQ, pitch deck, quarterly letter, draws from that source, the kind of governed workflow the[best RFP software for hedge funds](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/best-rfp-software-hedge-funds) is built to support. When the finance team refreshes an underlying figure, the update propagates to every downstream use automatically, with a timestamp recording when the change was approved and by whom.


Three structural requirements make this work in practice:


- Each quantitative figure must be tied to a specific source document and approval date, not a spreadsheet cell any analyst can edit without a change record.
- When a figure is updated, the prior version must be retained and attributable, so that if an LP asks why this cycle's net IRR differs from last cycle's, the answer is documented and not reconstructed after the fact.
- The IR team's DDQ responses and the finance team's data exports must draw from the same governed store, not parallel systems periodically synchronized by hand, which is the gap the best[RFP automation tools for asset managers](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/best-rfp-automation-tools-asset-managers) are designed to close.


The approval workflow is what closes the loop. A figure that reaches an LP submission without a documented approval chain is a compliance exposure under the SEC Marketing Rule, regardless of whether it is numerically correct. The chain of custody, who approved this figure, from which source, as of which date, must be traceable before the document leaves the firm.


## How AI-Generated DDQ Responses Can Introduce New Inconsistencies


The tools are not the problem. The problem is what they are allowed to see.


A general-purpose AI completing a DDQ will surface the most semantically relevant answer it finds in the document environment it has access to, which is exactly why purpose-built[AI agents for DDQ and RFP](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/ai-agents-ddq-rfp-asset-management) work differently in asset management. If that environment contains a prior-year questionnaire with an IRR figure that was later restated, the AI has no mechanism to know it is stale. It retrieves it, formats it cleanly, and returns an answer that reads as complete. The reviewer, trained to assess tone and structure instead of auditing individual figures against source documents, approves it.


The inconsistency that reaches the LP is not a hallucination. It is a correctly retrieved, cleanly formatted, confidently wrong number drawn from the wrong version of the fund's own data.


At small scale, a senior analyst reviewing ten questions can catch a figure that looks off. At scale, across forty questions, three concurrent submissions, and four analysts working from the same uncontrolled document store, the same failure repeats without triggering any flag. Two LPs receive materially different net IRR figures for the same fund vintage. Neither answer was invented. Both were retrieved from the GP's own files, from different source documents, on different days.


That is the specific risk AI introduces when the data layer beneath it is not version-controlled, approval-dated, and source-attributed. The AI retrieves faithfully from a fragmented environment, and faithful retrieval from fragmented data produces inconsistency at a rate that scales with submission volume.


Better prompting does not close this gap. Probabilistic generation cannot guarantee the same answer to the same question across two runs, two analysts, or two LPs, so consistency has to come from what the model is allowed to see. GovernGPT is designed to guarantee consistent responses by drawing on a single version-controlled answer set, replicating the deterministic behavior of a trained IR professional working from pre-approved content.

That distinction is what makes compliance sign-off possible: the line-level retrieved-versus-generated flag is the mechanism that makes the workflow formally auditable.


This matters most for performance data because the inconsistencies LP ODD teams and automated scoring models are built to catch are not fabricated numbers. They are correctly retrieved, cleanly formatted figures drawn from the wrong version of the GP's own files. GovernGPT's version-controlled document deprecation removes that failure mode at the data layer: outdated fund documents are retired before the AI ever sees them, so conflicting versions cannot surface interchangeably across submissions.


GovernGPT is built to act like a tier-1 fund's best RFP author. It writes verbatim pre-approved language wherever it exists (roughly 90% of pre-population, according to GovernGPT), uses AI only to bridge gaps between approved language, and limits the model's context to the firm's own vetted documents. When no approved answer exists for a question, it flags the gap instead of surfacing a plausible but unvetted number. That matters because the dangerous errors are subtle ones, like a stale IRR that reads as correct, and a full audit trail shows reviewers every step taken to reach each answer.


Performance data integrity becomes a property of the architecture, not a function of how carefully any individual analyst reviewed a given submission.


## Final Thoughts on Financial Due Diligence and Performance Data Integrity


LP diligence teams read your current DDQ against everything you've ever sent them. That's the operating reality your data governance needs to be built for. When figures shift between submissions without a documented explanation, the gap reads as a signal about your firm's rigor, far beyond a formatting inconsistency. Closing that gap starts with treating performance data as something that requires version control and approval chains, well beyond careful review alone.[GovernGPT](https://www.governgpt.com/) is designed to make that the default, so your submissions hold up whether the first reader is a human or an automated scoring model.


## FAQ


### How do I prevent AI from retrieving stale performance figures when auto-filling institutional DDQs?


The root cause is not the AI model. It is what the model is allowed to see. When multiple versions of a fund document coexist in an uncontrolled repository, any retrieval system will surface them interchangeably, producing figures that vary across submissions with no flag and no version conflict alert. The fix is upstream of the AI itself: each quantitative figure needs a governed approval date and as-of date, outdated documents must be retired before the AI ever queries them, and every refreshed data point must be surfaced visibly so reviewers know exactly what changed and when.


### What is financial due diligence on a private fund, and why does track-record consistency matter so much to institutional LPs?


Financial due diligence for a private fund is the systematic process by which institutional LPs test whether a GP's track record is internally consistent, methodologically sound, and reconcilable with independently verifiable sources: gross and net returns by vintage, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, fee and expense treatment, and valuation governance. Consistency matters because sophisticated LPs cross-reference current DDQ submissions against prior filings, pitch decks, quarterly letters, and their own proprietary databases going back several fund cycles; a net IRR that shifted between Fund IV and Fund V raises without a documented methodology explanation does not read as a refinement. It reads as a discrepancy, and two or more of those in the same cycle frequently trigger a data room reconciliation request before the recommendation advances.


### GovernGPT vs. Responsive or Loopio for a private equity IR team managing multiple fund vintages: which handles performance data integrity better?


Responsive and Loopio store QA pairs in flat, manually tagged content libraries that make maintaining version-controlled performance figures across multiple fund vintages impractical in practice: the tagging burden forces IR teams to collapse answer variants into a small canonical set, which is precisely the failure mode that produces inconsistent net IRR figures across LP submissions. GovernGPT's multi-dimensional knowledge graph assigns an approval date and as-of date to every quantitative figure, retires outdated fund documents before the AI queries them, and automatically propagates refreshed figures across all relevant DDQ answers with green markers so reviewers see exactly what changed, making performance data integrity a property of the architecture instead of a function of individual analyst review.


### Can AI reliably auto-fill ILPA DDQ performance templates without introducing cross-submission inconsistencies?


A general-purpose AI can auto-fill ILPA DDQ 2.0 performance templates, but without version-controlled source data it will retrieve the most semantically relevant figure it finds, which may be a net IRR from a prior fund vintage, a subscription-line-unadjusted return, or a realized value figure that has since been reclassified. The ILPA DDQ's fund-level and deal-level templates are designed to cross-reference each other, so a stale figure in one template will produce a reconciliation failure in the other that a diligent LP will catch. Reliable auto-fill requires a governed data layer where each figure is tied to a specific approved source document and approval date before the AI ever queries it.


### What does GovernGPT do differently to keep DDQ performance figures consistent across multiple LP submissions within the same fundraising cycle?


GovernGPT ties every quantitative figure to an approval date and an as-of date, so when the finance team uploads refreshed AUM, net IRR, or MOIC, those figures propagate automatically across all active DDQ and RFP answers with no manual re-entry per submission. Its color-coded traceability system marks refreshed quantitative data in green and AI-generated bridge sentences in purple, giving reviewers a line-level signal about exactly what the AI authored versus what was retrieved from approved precedent, which is the precise distinction that makes compliance sign-off possible. Outdated fund documents are retired from the live content library before the AI queries them, so conflicting versions cannot surface interchangeably across concurrent submissions to different LPs.
